A stenographer is a professional whose job is to listen to spoken words and write them down — accurately and in real time — as fast as people speak. The end goal is a written record of everything that was said.

Imagine you are in a courtroom. A lawyer asks a question. A witness answers. A judge makes a ruling. All of this happens at normal speaking speed — which is roughly 120 to 180 words per minute. A stenographer's job is to capture every single word of this conversation, word for word, as it happens, without missing anything.

That sounds nearly impossible if you think of regular writing or typing. This is exactly why stenographers use a special method to write so fast — called shorthand (or stenography).
How Do They Write So Fast?

Normal writing uses full words made of individual letters. That is slow. Stenographers instead use a system of symbols, abbreviations, and special marks that represent sounds or whole words. For example, instead of writing the word "government," a stenographer might draw a single curved symbol that takes half a second to write. These shorthand systems are like a secret code — compact, fast, and precise.

There are several shorthand systems (Gregg, Pitman, Teeline, etc.). Each system has its own set of symbols, but the purpose is the same: replace long words with short, quick marks.

Beyond the pen-and-paper method, many modern stenographers use a stenotype machine — a specialised keyboard with far fewer keys than a normal keyboard. Instead of pressing one key at a time, the stenographer presses several keys simultaneously (like a chord on a piano), and each combination represents a syllable, a word, or even a whole phrase. This is why experienced stenographers can record speech at 225 words per minute or more — far faster than the fastest typist on a regular keyboard.
What Happens After They Write It?

The shorthand notes or the machine output are not directly readable by ordinary people. So the stenographer's job doesn't end at recording — they also transcribe their notes, meaning they convert the shorthand symbols into plain, readable, full text. This final document is what becomes the official record.

With modern computer-aided transcription (CAT) software, the stenotype machine can automatically convert key-presses into text on a screen almost instantly, which is how live closed captions on television work.

1. Courts of Law
This is the most classic setting. During a trial, every question, every answer, every objection, and every ruling must be recorded exactly. A stenographer working in this role is often called a court reporter. The transcript they produce is a legal document — it can be used in appeals, reviews, and legal proceedings.

2. Legislative and Government Bodies
Parliaments, assemblies, and government committees often employ stenographers to produce official records of debates and proceedings.

3. Business and Corporate Settings
Executives sometimes dictate letters or memos to a stenographer, who takes them down in shorthand and later types them up. This was far more common in the 20th century, before email and voice recorders became standard.

4. Broadcasting and Captioning
Stenographers are behind the live closed captions you see on news broadcasts and live TV events. They listen and type in real time so that viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing can follow along.

5. Conferences and Public Events
Important speeches, medical proceedings, and depositions (formal interviews under oath) also use stenographers to create an exact record.
What Skills Does a Stenographer Need?

• Speed and accuracy — the ability to record speech at very high speeds without errors
  • Concentration — they must focus deeply for hours without losing track of anything
  • Strong language skills — they need a wide vocabulary to correctly recognise and transcribe technical, legal, or medical language
  • Good hearing — since everything depends on catching every word correctly
  • Reliability and impartiality — especially in legal settings, they must record exactly what was said, not what they think was meant
How Is a Stenographer Different from a Typist or Transcriptionist?

• A typist simply types text from a written source using a normal keyboard. They don't work in real time from speech.
  • A transcriptionist listens to pre-recorded audio and types it out at their own pace. They are not under the pressure of doing it live.
  • A stenographer works live, in real time, as words are being spoken, using specialised shorthand or a stenotype machine. This is the defining difference — the speed and the live nature of the work.
A Simple Way to Think About It

A stenographer is essentially a human real-time recorder and translator — they capture spoken words at the speed of speech and convert them into a permanent written document. They are the reason we have word-for-word records of courtroom dramas, parliamentary debates, and live broadcasts. Without stenographers, entire spoken events would vanish with no trace.
